events.source_title: Netherlands' Wellink survives resignation calls (Central Banking, via Risk.net)

events.summary: The coalition of Sebastian Kurz's People's Party and the Freedom Party announced plans in 2018 to reform banking supervision in Austria, which is split between the Financial Market Authority and the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, by stripping the central bank of its supervisory role. In April 2019 the OeNB publicly accused the government of seeking to undermine its financial independence. It objected to two things. The first was cost: it said supervision costs in Austria would rise under the new and more complicated structures, in particular because three new sections would be created inside the Finance Ministry. The second was the method of paying for that. The draft law provided for 95 percent of the central bank's profits to be paid to the federal government instead of the 90 percent then in force, which the bank said reduces its ability to build reserves and should therefore be seen as an encroachment on its financial independence. In its formal comments on the draft law, reported in May 2019, the OeNB said the independence of both the central bank and the banking watchdog was damaged by the plans. The Finance Ministry answered that it was following European best practice and what is common in many European countries, that a payout rate of 95 percent or more existed in countries including the Netherlands, and that the decision was structural and aimed at efficiency rather than personal. The reform did not take effect: the OeNB still carries out banking supervision and reported reorganising that function itself in 2025.
events.source_title: Austrian central bank says government threatens its financial independence (Reuters)

events.summary: In late June 2017 the Central Bank Law Commission, appointed by the Ministry of Finance and chaired by Svein Gjedrem, a former governor of Norges Bank and former secretary general of the ministry, proposed in its report NOU 2017:13 that responsibility for managing the Government Pension Fund Global - the oil fund, then about 8.1 trillion kroner and Europe's largest sovereign wealth fund - be transferred out of Norges Bank to a separate statutory entity. The fund is managed inside the bank by Norges Bank Investment Management, and removing it would have taken away the largest thing the bank does. Gjedrem's reasoning was that central banking and investment management differ in nature, that both had grown and now placed greater demands on the board, senior management and the organisation, and that separate bodies could tailor their skills to each task; he said the separation would have to be carried out soundly and must not otherwise affect the framework for the fund. The bank's own leadership was split in public from the fund's: governor Oystein Olsen wanted the fund kept inside Norges Bank, while the fund's chief executive Yngve Slyngstad was reported as believing it should be taken out. Norges Bank itself later described the separation proposal as the one that had drawn the most public attention of anything in the Commission's work. The Ministry of Finance rejected it, deciding the management should stay within the central bank, on the reasoning that Norges Bank enjoyed a high level of trust in Norway and internationally and that its performance in both roles had been good over time. The Storting passed the new Central Bank Act on 28 May 2019 and it entered into force on 1 January 2020, leaving the bank both core responsibilities and creating a separate monetary policy and financial stability committee. The question was raised again in the mandate of a later committee and the government withdrew it, saying the placement of the fund had recently been examined thoroughly, that there had been broad consensus in the Storting in 2018 and 2019 that management should remain within Norges Bank, and that stability in the management of the fund mattered.
events.source_title: Norway rejects idea of hiving off SWF management (IPE)

events.summary: On 9 December 2020 the Senate approved a bill, brought by Morena's Senate leader Ricardo Monreal, amending the Bank of Mexico Law to oblige the central bank to buy foreign banknotes and coins that commercial banks collect and cannot return to the country they came from. Banco de Mexico issued a statement the same day saying the draft decree would violate the autonomy the Constitution gives it, because the law itself would determine active operations the central bank is obliged to carry out, and those operations are high risk and could compromise its holdings of international reserves and its constitutional mandate to preserve the purchasing power of the currency. The bank set out the facts it said the Senate had ignored: foreign cash is less than 1 percent of remittances sent to Mexico, and of the 4.7 billion dollars in foreign cash that entered the country between January and September 2020, commercial banks placed or repatriated 98 percent through correspondent arrangements. It said foreign banknotes are treated as high risk under anti-money-laundering standards, that the decree would weaken those standards and spread the risk to the central bank itself, and that foreign authorities could respond by restricting the correspondents that process Mexican banks' foreign currency, or by restricting Banco de Mexico's own operations and agreements abroad. Governor Alejandro Diaz de Leon said in a radio interview that the bank could challenge the law in the Supreme Court and warned that the central bank could be sanctioned by foreign authorities, which could include being barred from transacting with counterparts abroad and the freezing or confiscation of international reserves. Monreal said it was no attack on the bank's autonomy and that Banco de Mexico had to be less conservative. The bill still needed the lower house, where the vote was put off to February 2021 and never carried; the obligation did not take effect.
events.source_title: Consideraciones sobre el proyecto de decreto de reformas a la Ley del Banco de Mexico para que adquiera moneda extranjera en efectivo, aprobado por el Senado de la Republica (Banco de Mexico press release, 9 December 2020)

events.summary: The Romanian government adopted emergency ordinance 114/2018 on 28 December 2018, imposing a 0.3 percent tax on banks' financial assets from 1 January 2019 and setting the rate of that tax by reference to ROBOR, the interbank money market rate. Because ROBOR moves with monetary policy, the tax rose as the National Bank of Romania raised rates. Governor Mugur Isarescu, appearing with the whole BNR board before Senate committees in February 2019, called it a tax on monetary policy that ties the central bank's hands and said that linking the asset tax to ROBOR is an attack on the independence of the National Bank. He had declined two earlier invitations from the committees; the MP who pressed for the hearings, Daniel Zamfir, had accused the bank of manipulating ROBOR, which Isarescu rejected, telling the committees that lower interest rates required low inflation and low budget and external deficits. Separately, a government adviser close to the ruling party leader, Darius Valcov, told Bloomberg that the central bank could cancel the tax by changing how ROBOR is calculated or scrapping the rate altogether, and that a decision would be taken with the central bank, which could change its internal market rules without parliamentary approval; the BNR's spokesman called the statement extremely confusing and said he did not know whom Valcov was speaking for. The European Central Bank wrote to the finance minister on 5 February 2019 saying it had not been consulted on the ordinance or on an earlier draft, contrary to its obligation under EU rules, and that the measure came with no impact assessment. On 26 March 2019 the government published amendments that removed the link to ROBOR, and the finance minister said the amendments had the BNR's approval.
events.source_title: Mugur Isarescu: Linking asset tax to ROBOR is an attack on the independence of the National Bank! (Business Review)

events.summary: Chile's Constitutional Convention, elected to write a replacement for the 1980 constitution, drafted new articles on the Banco Central de Chile in its Commission 6 on justice systems, autonomous oversight bodies and constitutional reform. On 5 April 2022 the bank's president Rosanna Costa wrote to the president of the Convention on behalf of the bank's Council, in official letter 114, setting out what the Council objected to. Its main objection was to the removal provision: the draft allowed one third of the members of Congress to ask the Supreme Court to remove councillors, which the bank said exposed the institution to a complex situation and to political judgements that would diminish its autonomy and its working. The Council asked that the power to request removal be limited to a majority of the councillors or to the President of the Republic, and that the existing organic law's standard be written in, so that a removed councillor's conduct must have been the main and direct cause of significant damage to the country's economy. It also asked that productive diversification be struck from the list of the bank's objectives, on the ground that it is not a monetary task, and that the rule in the current constitution's article 109 barring the bank from discriminating between parties be restored, as the draft had dropped it. On the governance articles the letter said changes should not diminish the effectiveness of the institution's autonomy, and it noted that appointment by the President of the Republic had not harmed the bank's autonomy. When the plenary voted on 4 May 2022 it approved the bank's existence and its autonomy but sent the articles on its powers, limits and the appointment of councillors back to committee for lack of the 103 votes needed. Voters rejected the draft constitution on 4 September 2022, so none of it took effect.
events.source_title: Oficio ORD. No 114 del Banco Central de Chile a la Presidenta de la Convencion Constitucional, 5 de abril de 2022

events.summary: Congress passed law 31143, protecting consumers of financial services from usury, by insistence on 11 March 2021 with 85 votes for, eight against and 12 abstentions, overriding the executive's objection; it was published on 18 March 2021. The law requires the Banco Central de Reserva del Peru to set maximum and minimum interest rates every six months for consumer loans up to two tax units, about 8,800 soles, and for loans to small and micro enterprises - taking a price-setting duty the bank did not want and had opposed in public. Governor Julio Velarde had stated the bank's position against limiting interest rates before the vote. When the bank published the methodology on 29 April 2021, setting the first ceiling at 83.4 percent a year from 10 May, it said in the same announcement that, notwithstanding the law, it considers rate ceilings not to be the most appropriate mechanism for improving credit conditions or deepening financial inclusion, because ceilings ration credit away from borrowers whose credit risk sits above the cap. In November 2021 the justice minister, Anibal Torres, publicly criticised Velarde for having come out against the law. The bank kept saying so with its own measurements: its central manager for economic studies, Adrian Armas, said the ceilings pushed informal and lower-income borrowers out of the formal system and into informal lending, and a bank study of the period from May 2021 to March 2024 estimated more than 542,000 people affected, 40 percent of them borrowers who left the financial system. Velarde later called the law almost useless and said it had fed loan rackets that had moved into criminal territory. The ceiling reached 112.98 percent a year for the period from November 2024. The Constitutional Court upheld the law as constitutional in case 00010-2021-AI; Congress approved repeal in a second vote in March 2025, and in July 2026 the government asked Congress for delegated powers to repeal it, citing the bank's technical opinion.
events.source_title: BCR: Tasa maxima de interes para el periodo mayo-octubre 2021 sera de 83.4% anual (El Peruano)
